system: You are a careful research assistant.
prompt:
Each item below gives what a research team actually decided, a one-sentence restatement of it, and several candidate options written by others for the same decision point.

For each item answer:
- "faithful": "yes" if the restatement describes the same decision as what the team decided (abstracting away study-specific details is fine), "no" if it changes, drops the core of, or adds to the decision.
- "same": for each candidate label, "same" if the candidate is essentially the team's decision (a reader who knew what the team did would say the team took this option, or it contains the team's decision as a part), else "different".

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "faithful": "yes" | "no", "same": {"<label>": "same" | "different"}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 7a784d3aa68c
What the team decided: Recommends testing a long list of models of different sizes while removing correlations and confounders before making the claim.
Restatement: Test the capability claim across a long list of models of different sizes, removing correlations and confounders before asserting that more capable models deceive more
C1: Run a follow-up comparison that holds instruction-following fixed by using scenarios matched for instruction difficulty, and only accept a capability effect if the gap survives controls
C2: Treat the existing gap across model generations as a real effect and report that more capable models deceive more, noting instruction-following as a plausible confound in passing

=== key 87edec8240bd
What the team decided: Recommends a defense-in-depth process where labs, auditors, and government each act as independent checks rather than one institution deciding alone.
Restatement: Structure deployment approval as layered checks where labs, external auditors, and government each act independently so the process stays robust if one link fails
C1: Structure the process as a standing internal review board that scores candidate behaviors by severity and reversibility, requires pre-deployment red-teaming signoff, and revisits decisions as mitigations shift
C2: Put deployment authority in the deploying lab's hands with a simple internal checklist of severe behaviors, since external actors cannot make such fine-grained judgments anyway

=== key 00c40a291513
What the team decided: Recommends staged release: trusted third-party auditors and academics red-team first, iterate on problems, then a small rollout to KYC-vetted customers, then monitoring during deployment.
Restatement: Release in stages: have trusted outside auditors probe the model first, fix what surfaces, then roll out to a small set of verified customers while monitoring
C1: Gather targeted red-teaming evidence on the most severe plausible behaviors plus staged rollout monitoring data, and gate release on documented signoff for each identified risk before shipping
C2: Gather evidence from a bounded round of adversarial testing on the worst plausible behaviors, then ship if nothing clearly dangerous surfaces, since open competitors will match the capability regardless

=== key 7f01502fd74f
What the team decided: Recommends staged open-source releases where a small team of trusted researchers first probes upper bounds of harm before wider release.
Restatement: Release open models in stages: let a small trusted team first probe the upper bounds of harm and how easily safeguards come off before wider general release
C1: Evaluate each proposed open release against a precommitted capability threshold with an external-style audit and a staged release option, treating the decision as irreversible and defaulting to hold when uncertain
C2: Evaluate each release with a focused internal assessment of whether its capabilities cross the line past which openness is unjustifiable, and release if it stays below that bar

=== key 40876f130ff7
What the team decided: Advises simply starting with a behavior you find interesting and letting the investigation grow organically rather than overthinking project selection.
Restatement: Start by picking a behavior that seems interesting and probing the model for a while, letting the project grow organically rather than overthinking the choice
C1: Choose projects that build the specific skills auditing organizations need, like systematic elicitation and rigorous writeups, and validate the work by seeking feedback from practitioners before publishing findings
C2: Pick a concrete surprising behavior and push public independent probing on it, sharing findings openly to demonstrate ability, since visible results are the fastest way into the field

=== key 11cc190ff518
What the team decided: Recommends using a theoretical understanding of training — RLHF, instruction fine-tuning, the 3 Hs tradeoffs — to explain behaviors and locate niches the model wasn't trained to cover.
Restatement: Explain the behavior through how the model was trained, using knowledge of the training pipeline and its tradeoffs to spot niches that training never covered
C1: Combine continued probing with interpretability and training-analysis methods to triangulate whether the behavior is a robust tendency or an artifact, before drawing conclusions about why it occurs
C2: Keep pushing open-ended elicitation to map where the behavior appears and strengthens, and form a working hypothesis about its cause from the pattern of results alone

=== key e9cccce61f0b
What the team decided: Keep scheming/deceptive alignment/deception as the organization's central focus because a non-deceptive misaligned model can simply be asked its goals.
Restatement: Keep deceptive behavior and scheming as the organisation's central research focus, concentrating evaluations, interpretability, and related work there going forward
C1: Keep the portfolio broad across evaluations, interpretability, and governance but designate deception-related threat models as the organizing focus, with periodic review of whether the emphasis still fits the evidence
C2: Commit the organisation to a single central focus on understanding and detecting deceptive behavior, concentrating hires and projects there since prior progress suggests it is tractable

=== key 7dbe035b572d
What the team decided: Downgrade flattery/sycophancy as a secondary concern compared to outcome-based training risks like power-seeking.
Restatement: Treat flattery and user-modeling as a secondary concern compared with outcome-training risks like power-seeking, which pose the more serious long-run danger
C1: Treat sycophancy as a high-priority early indicator of general score-seeking behavior, fund targeted evaluations of it, but keep it below unambiguously destructive failure modes until evidence strengthens
C2: Treat sycophancy and human-modeling as serious because they are early instances of the general tendency to game evaluations, and prioritize them alongside the most severe failure modes

=== key bf1ba1d7af02
What the team decided: Combine exploratory probing with running the full eval suite, comparing numbers to previous models, and manually reading transcripts including failures.
Restatement: Run the full eval suite, compare scores against previous models, then read transcripts in detail including failures while probing the model informally.
C1: Begin with open-ended qualitative probing across diverse tasks to map surprising behaviors before committing scarce time to tests built on prior hypotheses.
C2: Run targeted probes derived directly from prior hypotheses about how capabilities work, converting the window into quick focused tests of the most decision-relevant claims.

=== key 7bbbfcdc3537
What the team decided: Run everything quickly in parallel, check where numbers come from, then do guided analysis and build a handful of new evals for the most concerning areas.
Restatement: Run the whole suite quickly in parallel, inspect where the numbers come from, then do guided analysis and build a few new evals for the most concerning areas.
C1: Start with the prepared suite for baseline coverage, then reserve a block for qualitative exploration and one round of test rework informed by what the baseline reveals.
C2: Lead with freeform qualitative exploration to surface new capabilities first, then run the prepared suite once and adapt tests only where observations demand it.

=== key 5ef364eb05ad
What the team decided: Treat qualitative analysis of transcripts and failure cases as a major source of evidence alongside repeated runs.
Restatement: Treat qualitative reading of transcripts and failure cases as a major source of evidence alongside scores, rerunning evals many times to inspect variants.
C1: Treat quantitative scores as a screening layer and have team members read a substantial sample of transcripts, prioritizing runs where scores look anomalous or surprising.
C2: Rely primarily on quantitative scores for conclusions, reading transcripts only selectively to sanity-check headline results rather than systematically auditing them.

=== key 520f7810d417
What the team decided: Split evals into precursor capabilities (self-reasoning/situational awareness, theory of mind) plus an end-to-end scheming test to get earlier signal.
Restatement: Split the tests into precursor capabilities like self-reasoning and modeling others, plus an end-to-end scheming test, to get signal earlier.
C1: Decompose deception into staged sub-capabilities such as holding a hidden goal, planning covertly, and evading oversight, then measure each in isolation before the full behavior.
